Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have revolutionized the treatment landscape in solid tumors and are now standard of care across multiple cancer types.^{1} ICI therapy may offer long-lasting clinical benefit in advanced disease, as demonstrated in melanoma.^{2} Nevertheless, ICI resistance is a challenge, and response rates across all cancers are estimated to be about 20%.^{3} Mechanisms of resistance to ICIs are multifaceted, comprising both tumor cell intrinsic and extrinsic factors, but often not possible to unravel in clinical routine.^{4} Resistance phenotypes include primary resistance, in which tumors do not respond to ICI therapy, and secondary resistance, which implies tumor progression after initial clinical benefit.^{5}

text: Keywords: Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor, Biomarker, Immune related adverse event - irAE, Immunotherapy Phase I/II single-arm studies in advanced melanoma and gastrointestinal cancer have reported that resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) may be overcome by fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT). Applicability to other tumor types remains largely unexplored. Questions remain regarding patient and donor selection, and the FMT procedure. This single-arm study evaluated FMTs in combination with ICIs to patients progressing on ICIs. No objective responses were seen in 12 patients with four different types of cancer. Clinical benefit was demonstrated in one patient, remaining alive without further systemic treatment, and mixed responses were observed in two more patients. FMT was well tolerated. An activated T-cell signature in blood was associated with improved outcomes, while a myeloid-dominant immune milieu was unfavorable and not counteracted by FMT. This study does not support FMT as a salvage therapy in a non-biomarker-driven population of advanced heavily pretreated patients progressing on ICIs. However, the study suggests that FMT can safely be combined with ICI in patients with advanced cancer and that some patients may derive a benefit.
